Scope and reading plan

The current official syllabus combines Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations in Mathematics Unit 2. This chapter teaches the complex-number part; Chapter 3 develops quadratics further. The source also asks a few supporting geometry and complex-power questions, so the needed ideas are explained here.

Our route: number meaning → plane and distance → algebra → angle and rotation → powers and roots → loci → source problems.

Important for JEE Main is a teaching priority label. It is not a measured formula-frequency claim.

Source convention to know before Q33: the source treats “purely imaginary” as having real part zero, including the value zero. Some books reserve the words for a nonzero imaginary number. Q33(i) gives zero when z=−1z=-1z=−1; the solution states this corner case. The principal value convention for iii^iii is also explained there. Do not hide either convention.

Formula and concept bank

Concept C01 — Why do we need a complex number?

Important for JEE Main. No real number has square −1-1−1: squaring a real number gives a nonnegative answer. We introduce a new number iii with

i2=−1.\boxed{i^2=-1}.i2=−1​.

A complex number has the form

z=x+iy,x,y∈R.\boxed{z=x+iy,\qquad x,y\in\mathbb R}.z=x+iy,x,y∈R​.

The letters x,yx,yx,y are real numbers. The symbol iii is fixed, just as π\piπ is fixed. The letter zzz stands for the whole complex number.

  • Re⁡z=x\operatorname{Re}z=xRez=x is the real part.
  • Im⁡z=y\operatorname{Im}z=yImz=y is the imaginary part. It is the real coefficient yyy, not iyiyiy.

For z=3−4iz=3-4iz=3−4i, Re⁡z=3\operatorname{Re}z=3Rez=3 and Im⁡z=−4\operatorname{Im}z=-4Imz=−4. For the real number 5=5+0i5=5+0i5=5+0i, the imaginary part is zero. Every real number is also a complex number.

Two complex numbers are equal exactly when both parts match:

x+iy=u+iv  ⟺  x=u and y=v.x+iy=u+iv\iff x=u\text{ and }y=v.x+iy=u+iv⟺x=u and y=v.

Why? A change along one coordinate cannot be repaired by a change along the other. For example, 2+3i2+3i2+3i and 3+2i3+2i3+2i are different.

Do not order complex numbers with >>> or <<<. A question can compare their real parts, imaginary parts, or lengths. It cannot use the ordinary real-number order on arbitrary complex numbers.

Concept C02 — The Argand plane: turn the number into a point

Important for JEE Main. Draw a horizontal real axis and a vertical imaginary axis. The number x+iyx+iyx+iy is the point P(x,y)P(x,y)P(x,y). This picture is the Argand plane.

Read the picture: 3+2i3+2i3+2i means move 333 units right and 222 units up from the origin OOO. The arrow OPOPOP has the same two components.

If z1z_1z1​ represents PPP and z2z_2z2​ represents QQQ, then

z2−z1 represents the movement from P to Q.\boxed{z_2-z_1\text{ represents the movement from }P\text{ to }Q}.z2​−z1​ represents the movement from P to Q​.

It is destination minus start. For example,

(4+3i)−(1+i)=3+2i.(4+3i)-(1+i)=3+2i.(4+3i)−(1+i)=3+2i.

Adding complex numbers adds their two components:

(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v).(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v).(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v).

This is also arrow addition. Notice that the point QQQ and the movement PQPQPQ need not be the same complex number. This distinction matters when rotating about a point other than the origin.

The distance between the points is the length of the difference:

PQ=∣z2−z1∣.\boxed{PQ=|z_2-z_1|}.PQ=∣z2​−z1​∣​.

For P(1,1)P(1,1)P(1,1) and Q(4,3)Q(4,3)Q(4,3), this distance is 32+22=13\sqrt{3^2+2^2}=\sqrt{13}32+22​=13​.

Concept C03 — Powers of iii repeat after four steps

Important for JEE Main. Start from i2=−1i^2=-1i2=−1 and multiply by iii each time:

i0=1,i1=i,i2=−1,i3=−i,i4=1.i^0=1,\quad i^1=i,\quad i^2=-1,\quad i^3=-i,\quad i^4=1.i0=1,i1=i,i2=−1,i3=−i,i4=1.

The next power is iii again. Thus

i4k=1,i4k+1=i,i4k+2=−1,i4k+3=−i.\boxed{i^{4k}=1,\quad i^{4k+1}=i,\quad i^{4k+2}=-1,\quad i^{4k+3}=-i}.i4k=1,i4k+1=i,i4k+2=−1,i4k+3=−i​.

Read the cycle: multiplying by iii makes a 90∘90^\circ90∘ anticlockwise turn. Four such turns bring us back.

Question clue: a huge integer power of iii only needs the remainder after division by 444. For example, 101=4(25)+1101=4(25)+1101=4(25)+1, so i101=ii^{101}=ii101=i.

For a sum, also notice

1+i−1−i=0.\boxed{1+i-1-i=0}.1+i−1−i=0​.

Any four consecutive integer powers sum to zero. Q1 therefore needs only the terms left after complete groups of four.

Negative integer powers follow the same cycle because 1/i=−i1/i=-i1/i=−i. For example, i−1=−ii^{-1}=-ii−1=−i and i−2=−1i^{-2}=-1i−2=−1. The rule is for integer powers; fractional or complex powers need extra conventions.

Concept C04 — Arithmetic and the conjugate

Important for JEE Main. Multiply using ordinary brackets, then replace i2i^2i2 by −1-1−1:

(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu−yv)+i(xv+yu).(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu).(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu−yv)+i(xv+yu).

For example,

(2+i)(3−i)=6−2i+3i−i2=7+i.(2+i)(3-i)=6-2i+3i-i^2=7+i.(2+i)(3−i)=6−2i+3i−i2=7+i.

The conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part:

z‾=x−iy.\boxed{\overline z=x-iy}.z=x−iy​.

It reflects the point across the real axis.

Adding or subtracting the reflected pair gives

z+z‾=2Re⁡z,z−z‾=2iIm⁡z.\boxed{z+\overline z=2\operatorname{Re}z},\qquad \boxed{z-\overline z=2i\operatorname{Im}z}.z+z=2Rez​,z−z=2iImz​.

Multiplying gives

zz‾=x2+y2=∣z∣2.\boxed{z\overline z=x^2+y^2=|z|^2}.zz=x2+y2=∣z∣2​.

This number is real and nonnegative. It is zero only when z=0z=0z=0.

Division: make the denominator real. For w≠0w\ne0w=0,

zw=zw‾∣w∣2,1z=z‾∣z∣2(z≠0).\boxed{\frac zw=\frac{z\overline w}{|w|^2}},\qquad \boxed{\frac1z=\frac{\overline z}{|z|^2}\quad(z\ne0)}.wz​=∣w∣2zw​​,z1​=∣z∣2z​(z=0)​.

Example:

1+i1−i=(1+i)2(1−i)(1+i)=2i2=i.\frac{1+i}{1-i} =\frac{(1+i)^2}{(1-i)(1+i)} =\frac{2i}{2}=i.1−i1+i​=(1−i)(1+i)(1+i)2​=22i​=i.

We used the conjugate of the denominator, not an arbitrary extra factor.

Useful rules:

z+w‾=z‾+w‾,zw‾=z‾ w‾,zw‾=z‾w‾ (w≠0).\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\quad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\quad \overline{\frac zw}=\frac{\overline z}{\overline w}\ (w\ne0).z+w​=z+w,zw=zw,wz​​=wz​ (w=0).

Tests, with the zero convention stated: zzz is real iff z=z‾z=\overline zz=z. Its real part is zero iff z=−z‾z=-\overline zz=−z. Some texts call only the nonzero members of the second group “purely imaginary”; the algebraic test itself includes zero.

Concept C05 — Modulus means length, not the whole number

Important for JEE Main. For z=x+iyz=x+iyz=x+iy,

∣z∣=x2+y2.\boxed{|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}.∣z∣=x2+y2​​.

This is the distance from OOO to P(x,y)P(x,y)P(x,y), by Pythagoras. It is always a nonnegative real number. Thus ∣3+4i∣=5|3+4i|=5∣3+4i∣=5.

The vertical bars here mean complex-number length. In Chapter 1, bars around a set meant its number of members. Read the object inside.

∣z∣2=zz‾,∣z‾∣=∣−z∣=∣z∣,\boxed{|z|^2=z\overline z},\qquad |\overline z|=|-z|=|z|,∣z∣2=zz​,∣z∣=∣−z∣=∣z∣, ∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣,∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣(w≠0).\boxed{|zw|=|z||w|},\qquad \boxed{\left|\frac zw\right|=\frac{|z|}{|w|}\quad(w\ne0)}.∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣​,​wz​​=∣w∣∣z∣​(w=0)​.

If only a modulus is asked, these often avoid a long complex division.

Lengths of a sum and difference. Expanding with conjugates gives

∣z+w∣2=∣z∣2+∣w∣2+2Re⁡(zw‾),|z+w|^2=|z|^2+|w|^2+2\operatorname{Re}(z\overline w),∣z+w∣2=∣z∣2+∣w∣2+2Re(zw), ∣z−w∣2=∣z∣2+∣w∣2−2Re⁡(zw‾).|z-w|^2=|z|^2+|w|^2-2\operatorname{Re}(z\overline w).∣z−w∣2=∣z∣2+∣w∣2−2Re(zw).

Add them and the mixed parts cancel:

∣z+w∣2+∣z−w∣2=2(∣z∣2+∣w∣2).\boxed{|z+w|^2+|z-w|^2=2(|z|^2+|w|^2)}.∣z+w∣2+∣z−w∣2=2(∣z∣2+∣w∣2)​.

This is the parallelogram identity. Think of the sum and difference as its two diagonals. Q17 asks for exactly this missing partner.

Triangle inequalities — Important for JEE Main.

∣∣z∣−∣w∣∣≤∣z−w∣≤∣z∣+∣w∣.\boxed{\big||z|-|w|\big|\le|z-w|\le|z|+|w|}.​∣z∣−∣w∣​≤∣z−w∣≤∣z∣+∣w∣​.

The corresponding bound for ∣z+w∣|z+w|∣z+w∣ is the same. A direct route cannot be longer than a two-step route; the difference of two lengths cannot exceed the distance between their endpoints.

Equality needs a suitable direction, not just suitable lengths. For the upper sum bound ∣z+w∣=∣z∣+∣w∣|z+w|=|z|+|w|∣z+w∣=∣z∣+∣w∣, two nonzero arrows must point the same way. For the lower sum bound they point opposite ways. Zero arrows are separate equality cases.

Cauchy–Schwarz — Important for JEE Main. For real x,y,u,vx,y,u,vx,y,u,v,

(xu+yv)2≤(x2+y2)(u2+v2).(xu+yv)^2\le(x^2+y^2)(u^2+v^2).(xu+yv)2≤(x2+y2)(u2+v2).

Here xu+yv=Re⁡((x+iy)(u−iv))xu+yv=\operatorname{Re}((x+iy)(u-iv))xu+yv=Re((x+iy)(u−iv)). Therefore

∣Re⁡(zw‾)∣≤∣z∣∣w∣.\boxed{|\operatorname{Re}(z\overline w)|\le|z||w|}.∣Re(zw)∣≤∣z∣∣w∣​.

The expression inside the real part measures how much two arrows point along each other. If the arrows are perpendicular, that real part is zero. This is the complex-number version of the dot-product connection. Use it for length bounds, but check whether an equality direction can actually occur.

Concept C06 — Argument is direction; principal argument selects one angle

Important for JEE Main. For z≠0z\ne0z=0, an argument is an angle of the arrow OPOPOP from the positive real axis. Anticlockwise angles are positive; clockwise angles are negative.

Adding a full turn changes the angle but not the point:

arg⁡z=θ+2kπ,k∈Z.\arg z=\theta+2k\pi,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.argz=θ+2kπ,k∈Z.

Here we use the principal argument

Arg⁡z∈(−π,π].\boxed{\operatorname{Arg}z\in(-\pi,\pi]}.Argz∈(−π,π]​.

The origin has no direction: Arg⁡0\operatorname{Arg}0Arg0 is undefined. The positive real axis has principal angle 000, and the negative real axis has π\piπ in our convention.

Why not just use inverse tangent? The ratio y/xy/xy/x alone loses the quadrant. Both (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and (−1,−1)(-1,-1)(−1,−1) have the same ratio, but their directions differ.

First locate the quadrant. Then use the small reference angle

α=tan⁡−1∣y/x∣(x≠0).\alpha=\tan^{-1}|y/x|\quad(x\ne0).α=tan−1∣y/x∣(x=0).
Position Principal angle
Quadrant I α\alphaα
Quadrant II π−α\pi-\alphaπ−α
Quadrant III −π+α-\pi+\alpha−π+α
Quadrant IV −α-\alpha−α
Positive / negative imaginary axis π/2\pi/2π/2 / −π/2-\pi/2−π/2

For −3+i-\sqrt3+i−3​+i, the reference angle is π/6\pi/6π/6 but the point is in quadrant II. Its principal angle is π−π/6=5π/6\pi-\pi/6=5\pi/6π−π/6=5π/6.

Angles in complex polar formulas use radians: π\piπ radians equals 180∘180^\circ180∘.

Concept C07 — Polar form separates length and direction

Important for JEE Main. A point at distance rrr and angle θ\thetaθ has coordinates

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ.x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta.x=rcosθ,y=rsinθ.

Thus

z=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)=r cis⁡θ,r=∣z∣.\boxed{z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=r\,\operatorname{cis}\theta}, \qquad r=|z|.z=r(cosθ+isinθ)=rcisθ​,r=∣z∣.

The abbreviation cis⁡θ\operatorname{cis}\thetacisθ means exactly cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ\cos\theta+i\sin\thetacosθ+isinθ.

We may also write cis⁡θ=eiθ\operatorname{cis}\theta=e^{i\theta}cisθ=eiθ using Euler's identity. In these questions that notation is a compact way to write the same direction.

Which form should I use?

  • Use x+iyx+iyx+iy for comparing real/imaginary parts, conjugates, and simple locus equations.
  • Use rcis⁡θr\operatorname{cis}\thetarcisθ for large powers, roots, and rotation.
  • Use the point/distance view for circles, nearest points, and triangle geometry.

For example, 1+i31+i\sqrt31+i3​ has r=2r=2r=2 and θ=π/3\theta=\pi/3θ=π/3, so its polar form is 2cis⁡(π/3)2\operatorname{cis}(\pi/3)2cis(π/3). Expanding its twelfth power would create many terms; the polar form keeps just a length and an angle.

For z=0z=0z=0, the length is zero and the polar direction is not unique. Do not assign it an argument just because the expression 0cis⁡θ0\operatorname{cis}\theta0cisθ can be written.

Concept C08 — Multiplication scales and turns an arrow

Important for JEE Main. The angle-addition identities give

(rcis⁡α)(scis⁡β)=rscis⁡(α+β).(r\operatorname{cis}\alpha)(s\operatorname{cis}\beta) =rs\operatorname{cis}(\alpha+\beta).(rcisα)(scisβ)=rscis(α+β).

So multiplication multiplies lengths and adds directions. Division, for a nonzero divisor, divides lengths and subtracts directions:

rcis⁡αscis⁡β=rscis⁡(α−β).\frac{r\operatorname{cis}\alpha}{s\operatorname{cis}\beta} =\frac rs\operatorname{cis}(\alpha-\beta).scisβrcisα​=sr​cis(α−β).

Multiplication by i=cis⁡(π/2)i=\operatorname{cis}(\pi/2)i=cis(π/2) turns an arrow 90∘90^\circ90∘ anticlockwise without changing its length. In components,

i(x+iy)=−y+ix:(x,y)⟼(−y,x).\boxed{i(x+iy)=-y+ix:\quad(x,y)\longmapsto(-y,x)}.i(x+iy)=−y+ix:(x,y)⟼(−y,x)​.

Multiplication by −i-i−i turns clockwise; by −1-1−1 makes a half-turn.

Rotation about a point ccc: first work with the movement from ccc:

znew=c+(z−c)cis⁡θ.\boxed{z_{\text{new}}=c+(z-c)\operatorname{cis}\theta}.znew​=c+(z−c)cisθ​.

Read the three actions: subtract ccc → turn the displacement → add ccc back. Multiplying zzz directly would rotate about the origin, which is a different centre.

Principal angles must be brought back into the chosen interval.

Arg⁡(zw)≡Arg⁡z+Arg⁡w(mod2π).\operatorname{Arg}(zw)\equiv \operatorname{Arg}z+\operatorname{Arg}w\pmod{2\pi}.Arg(zw)≡Argz+Argw(mod2π).

The symbol ≡(mod2π)\equiv\pmod{2\pi}≡(mod2π) means the two angles may differ by whole turns. It is not always an ordinary equality. For example, z=w=−1z=w=-1z=w=−1 gives angle sum 2π2\pi2π, but zw=1zw=1zw=1 has principal angle 000.

For division use the same whole-turn adjustment. For conjugation, the direction changes sign; if this gives −π-\pi−π, write π\piπ in our principal interval.

Concept C09 — Powers and all the roots

Important for JEE Main. Repeated multiplication repeats the length-and-turn rule:

(rcis⁡θ)n=rncis⁡(nθ)\boxed{(r\operatorname{cis}\theta)^n=r^n\operatorname{cis}(n\theta)}(rcisθ)n=rncis(nθ)​

for integers nnn; for negative nnn, require r>0r>0r>0. This is de Moivre's formula.

Now solve zn=wz^n=wzn=w, where nnn is a positive integer and w=Rcis⁡ϕ≠0w=R\operatorname{cis}\phi\ne0w=Rcisϕ=0. The length must be R1/nR^{1/n}R1/n. The angle after multiplication by nnn can be ϕ\phiϕ or ϕ+2π\phi+2\piϕ+2π or another whole-turn version:

zk=R1/ncis⁡ ⁣(ϕ+2kπn),k=0,1,…,n−1.\boxed{z_k=R^{1/n}\operatorname{cis}\!\left(\frac{\phi+2k\pi}{n}\right), \quad k=0,1,\ldots,n-1}.zk​=R1/ncis(nϕ+2kπ​),k=0,1,…,n−1​.

Why all nnn answers? Adding 2π2\pi2π before dividing by nnn creates an angle gap 2π/n2\pi/n2π/n. Stopping after the first angle loses the other roots. After nnn steps the directions repeat.

All roots lie on one circle, equally spaced in angle: a regular polygon when n≥3n\ge3n≥3. For w=0w=0w=0, the only distinct solution is z=0z=0z=0; do not claim nnn distinct points.

Root product: the product of all nnn roots of zn=wz^n=wzn=w is (−1)n−1w(-1)^{n-1}w(−1)n−1w. This follows by comparing the constant term of zn−wz^n-wzn−w with the product form.

Concept C10 — Roots of unity and the useful cube-root identities

Important for JEE Main. A root of unity means a solution of zn=1z^n=1zn=1:

zk=cis⁡2kπn,k=0,…,n−1.\boxed{z_k=\operatorname{cis}\frac{2k\pi}{n},\quad k=0,\ldots,n-1}.zk​=cisn2kπ​,k=0,…,n−1​.

All have modulus 111. One root is 111 itself. Their product is (−1)n−1(-1)^{n-1}(−1)n−1. For n>1n>1n>1, their sum is zero: equally spaced arrows balance at the origin.

The non-real cube roots are usually called ω,ω2\omega,\omega^2ω,ω2. We may choose

ω=−12+32i,ω2=−12−32i.\omega=-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i,\qquad \omega^2=-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i.ω=−21​+23​​i,ω2=−21​−23​​i.

From (z3−1)=(z−1)(z2+z+1)(z^3-1)=(z-1)(z^2+z+1)(z3−1)=(z−1)(z2+z+1),

ω3=1,1+ω+ω2=0,ωω2=1,ω‾=ω2.\boxed{\omega^3=1,\quad1+\omega+\omega^2=0,\quad \omega\omega^2=1,\quad\overline\omega=\omega^2}.ω3=1,1+ω+ω2=0,ωω2=1,ω=ω2​.

Therefore

ω+ω2=−1,1ω=ω2,1ω2=ω,\omega+\omega^2=-1,\quad \frac1\omega=\omega^2,\quad\frac1{\omega^2}=\omega,ω+ω2=−1,ω1​=ω2,ω21​=ω, (1−ω)(1−ω2)=3,∣1−ω∣=3.\boxed{(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)=3},\qquad |1-\omega|=\sqrt3.(1−ω)(1−ω2)=3​,∣1−ω∣=3​.

To get the last product, expand only this short pair:

1−(ω+ω2)+ω3=1−(−1)+1=3.1-(\omega+\omega^2)+\omega^3=1-(-1)+1=3.1−(ω+ω2)+ω3=1−(−1)+1=3.

Recognition clue: large powers of ω\omegaω need only their remainder modulo 333. Reduce the exponents before a long expansion.

More generally, for zn=1z^n=1zn=1 and z≠1z\ne1z=1,

1+z+z2+⋯+zn−1=0.\boxed{1+z+z^2+\cdots+z^{n-1}=0}.1+z+z2+⋯+zn−1=0​.

Multiply the sum by 1−z1-z1−z to get 1−zn=01-z^n=01−zn=0. The condition z≠1z\ne1z=1 is needed for division by 1−z1-z1−z. If z=1z=1z=1, the sum is nnn instead.

For a primitive root ζ=cis⁡(2π/n)\zeta=\operatorname{cis}(2\pi/n)ζ=cis(2π/n),

∑k=0n−1ζmk={n,n∣m,0,n∤m.\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\zeta^{mk} =\begin{cases}n,&n\mid m,\\0,&n\nmid m.\end{cases}k=0∑n−1​ζmk={n,0,​n∣m,n∤m.​

Here n∣mn\mid mn∣m means mmm is a multiple of nnn. This is the same geometric-sum argument. Do not assume an arbitrary nnnth root is primitive; “primitive” means its powers visit all nnn roots before returning to 111.

Concept C11 — A locus is the set of every allowed position

Important for JEE Main. A locus is not one point. It is all points satisfying a rule. First translate the rule into distances or directions.

Complex statement Picture
∣z−c∣=r|z-c|=r∣z−c∣=r, r>0r>0r>0 Circle, centre ccc, radius rrr.
∣z−c∣≤r|z-c|\le r∣z−c∣≤r Circle together with its inside: a closed disk.
∣z−c∣<r|z-c|<r∣z−c∣<r Inside only; boundary excluded.
∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣|z-a|=|z-b|∣z−a∣=∣z−b∣, a≠ba\ne ba=b Perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a,ba,ba,b.
Re⁡z=h\operatorname{Re}z=hRez=h Vertical line x=hx=hx=h.
Im⁡z=k\operatorname{Im}z=kImz=k Horizontal line y=ky=ky=k.
Arg⁡(z−c)=θ\operatorname{Arg}(z-c)=\thetaArg(z−c)=θ Ray from ccc in direction θ\thetaθ, with ccc excluded.

For r=0r=0r=0, ∣z−c∣=0|z-c|=0∣z−c∣=0 is just the point ccc. A negative proposed radius gives no points.

Read the fixed points correctly: ∣z+i∣=∣z−(−i)∣|z+i|=|z-(-i)|∣z+i∣=∣z−(−i)∣ is distance from −i-i−i, not from iii.

If z=x+iyz=x+iyz=x+iy and c=a+ibc=a+ibc=a+ib,

∣z−c∣2=(x−a)2+(y−b)2.|z-c|^2=(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2.∣z−c∣2=(x−a)2+(y−b)2.

Both distances are nonnegative, so squaring an equality of distances is safe. It often cancels the x2+y2x^2+y^2x2+y2 terms and leaves a line.

Fixed ratio of distances — Important for JEE Main. Suppose a,ba,ba,b are two distinct fixed points and

∣z−a∣=k∣z−b∣,k>0.|z-a|=k|z-b|,\qquad k>0.∣z−a∣=k∣z−b∣,k>0.

For k=1k=1k=1, this is the perpendicular bisector already explained. For k≠1k\ne1k=1, it is a circle with

centre c=a−k2b1−k2,radius r=k∣a−b∣∣1−k2∣.\boxed{\text{centre }c=\frac{a-k^2b}{1-k^2},\qquad \text{radius }r=\frac{k|a-b|}{|1-k^2|}}.centre c=1−k2a−k2b​,radius r=∣1−k2∣k∣a−b∣​​.

The letters a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c here represent complex points; k,rk,rk,r are real lengths or ratios. The result comes from squaring the two distances and completing squares. It is often called an Apollonius circle; its meaning is simply a fixed distance ratio.

For example, ∣z∣=2∣z−2∣|z|=2|z-2|∣z∣=2∣z−2∣ gives

x2+y2=4((x−2)2+y2)⟹(x−8/3)2+y2=(4/3)2.x^2+y^2=4\big((x-2)^2+y^2\big) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x-8/3)^2+y^2=(4/3)^2.x2+y2=4((x−2)2+y2)⟹(x−8/3)2+y2=(4/3)2.

Read the example: distance to A=0A=0A=0 is twice distance to B=2B=2B=2 at every point of the circle. If the original statement is written as a quotient, retain its denominator restriction. Here z=2z=2z=2 is not on the circle anyway.

Distance from the origin to a circle. If ∣z−c∣=r|z-c|=r∣z−c∣=r,

min⁡∣z∣=∣∣c∣−r∣,max⁡∣z∣=∣c∣+r.\boxed{\min|z|=\big||c|-r\big|,\qquad\max|z|=|c|+r}.min∣z∣=​∣c∣−r​,max∣z∣=∣c∣+r​.

For distance from another fixed point aaa, shift the origin to aaa:

min⁡∣z−a∣=∣∣c−a∣−r∣,max⁡∣z−a∣=∣c−a∣+r.\boxed{\min|z-a|=\big||c-a|-r\big|,\qquad \max|z-a|=|c-a|+r}.min∣z−a∣=​∣c−a∣−r​,max∣z−a∣=∣c−a∣+r​.

If the target is ∣Az+B∣|Az+B|∣Az+B∣ with A≠0A\ne0A=0, factor it as ∣A∣ ∣z+B/A∣|A|\,|z+B/A|∣A∣∣z+B/A∣: it is a scaled distance from −B/A-B/A−B/A. This connects a seemingly algebraic target to the same circle picture.

The centre, origin, and extreme points lie on the same straight line. If the origin lies inside the circle, the nearest boundary point is still at distance r−∣c∣r-|c|r−∣c∣.

Circle and disk are different. For a disk ∣z−c∣≤r|z-c|\le r∣z−c∣≤r, the minimum is max⁡(0,∣c∣−r)\max(0,|c|-r)max(0,∣c∣−r), because the origin itself is allowed when it lies inside. For the boundary circle, it may not be allowed.

Concept C12 — An angle condition needs both the line and its direction

Important for JEE Main. For z≠a,bz\ne a,bz=a,b, the quotient

z−az−b\frac{z-a}{z-b}z−bz−a​

compares the directions of the two arrows from the fixed points a,ba,ba,b to zzz. Its argument is the direction of z−az-az−a minus the direction of z−bz-bz−b, with whole-turn adjustment.

If the principal argument of a nonzero number www is π/2\pi/2π/2, then

Re⁡w=0,Im⁡w>0.\boxed{\operatorname{Re}w=0,\qquad\operatorname{Im}w>0}.Rew=0,Imw>0​.

The condition is not merely “real part zero”: the negative imaginary axis has angle −π/2-\pi/2−π/2, and zero has no argument.

For the source example, let z=x+iyz=x+iyz=x+iy. Multiply by the conjugate of z+1z+1z+1:

z−1z+1=(x−1+iy)(x+1−iy)(x+1)2+y2=x2+y2−1+2iy(x+1)2+y2.\frac{z-1}{z+1} =\frac{(x-1+iy)(x+1-iy)}{(x+1)^2+y^2} =\frac{x^2+y^2-1+2iy}{(x+1)^2+y^2}.z+1z−1​=(x+1)2+y2(x−1+iy)(x+1−iy)​=(x+1)2+y2x2+y2−1+2iy​.

The denominator is positive away from z=−1z=-1z=−1. Therefore angle π/2\pi/2π/2 requires

x2+y2=1,y>0.x^2+y^2=1,\qquad y>0.x2+y2=1,y>0.

Read the picture: the circle gives the right angle; the sign chooses the upper half. At z=1z=1z=1 the quotient is zero, and at z=−1z=-1z=−1 it is undefined. Neither endpoint belongs.

An argument condition can select an arc or a ray rather than a full circle or full line. Always keep the direction condition.

Concept C13 — A sum of two distances: ellipse, segment, or no points

Important for JEE Main as a geometry connection. Let A,BA,BA,B be distinct fixed points a distance 2c>02c>02c>0 apart. Consider

PA+PB=2a.PA+PB=2a.PA+PB=2a.

The two-step route from AAA through PPP to BBB cannot be shorter than ABABAB.

  • If 2a<2c2a<2c2a<2c, there are no points.
  • If 2a=2c2a=2c2a=2c, the route is straight without going past an endpoint: PPP lies on the closed segment ABABAB.
  • If 2a>2c2a>2c2a>2c, the points form a nondegenerate ellipse.

The two fixed points are the foci. The centre is their midpoint. The longer diameter through them is the major axis, of length 2a2a2a. The shorter diameter is 2b2b2b, with

b2=a2−c2,e=ca,0<e<1.\boxed{b^2=a^2-c^2,\qquad e=\frac ca,\quad0<e<1}.b2=a2−c2,e=ac​,0<e<1​.

The number eee is eccentricity. It compares the focus distance with the major semi-axis: it tells us how stretched the ellipse is.

For foci −1,1-1,1−1,1 and distance sum 444, c=1c=1c=1 and a=2a=2a=2, so e=1/2e=1/2e=1/2. The equation is x2/4+y2/3=1x^2/4+y^2/3=1x2/4+y2/3=1.

Trap: seeing a sum of distances does not by itself prove a nondegenerate ellipse. Compare the constant with the distance between the foci. Source Q19 tests exactly this.

Concept C14 — Equations mixing zzz, z‾\overline zz, and ∣z∣|z|∣z∣

Important for JEE Main. There are two especially useful routes.

Route 1: compare lengths first. If zm=z‾z^m=\overline zzm=z with integer m≥2m\ge2m≥2, put r=∣z∣r=|z|r=∣z∣. Taking moduli gives

rm=r⟹r=0 or rm−1=1.r^m=r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=0\text{ or }r^{m-1}=1.rm=r⟹r=0 or rm−1=1.

Since rrr is nonnegative, the nonzero case has r=1r=1r=1. Then z‾=1/z\overline z=1/zz=1/z, so

zm=1z⟹zm+1=1.z^m=\frac1z\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z^{m+1}=1.zm=z1​⟹zm+1=1.

Hence there are m+1m+1m+1 unit-circle solutions and the separate solution zero:

number of distinct solutions of zm=z‾=m+2.\boxed{\text{number of distinct solutions of }z^m=\overline z=m+2}.number of distinct solutions of zm=z=m+2​.

This shortcut assumes exactly the stated equation and m≥2m\ge2m≥2. If you divide by zzz at the start, you lose the zero solution. If m=1m=1m=1, all real numbers solve the equation; the formula does not apply.

Route 2: compare real and imaginary parts. For an equation such as ∣z∣−z=1+2i|z|-z=1+2i∣z∣−z=1+2i, the modulus has no imaginary part. Put z=x+iyz=x+iyz=x+iy:

x2+y2−x−iy=1+2i.\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-x-iy=1+2i.x2+y2​−x−iy=1+2i.

Read the imaginary equation first: −y=2-y=2−y=2. This reduces the rest to one real unknown. Before squaring a root equation, keep its sign condition and substitute the final candidate back.

Concept C15 — Square roots of a complex number

Important for JEE Main. Suppose

(a+ib)2=u+iv,a,b,u,v∈R.(a+ib)^2=u+iv,\qquad a,b,u,v\in\mathbb R.(a+ib)2=u+iv,a,b,u,v∈R.

Expanding gives

a2−b2=u,2ab=v.\boxed{a^2-b^2=u,\qquad2ab=v}.a2−b2=u,2ab=v​.

Also, lengths give

a2+b2=∣u+iv∣=u2+v2=R.a^2+b^2=|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}=R.a2+b2=∣u+iv∣=u2+v2​=R.

Adding and subtracting,

a2=R+u2,b2=R−u2.\boxed{a^2=\frac{R+u}{2},\qquad b^2=\frac{R-u}{2}}.a2=2R+u​,b2=2R−u​​.

The sign of 2ab=v2ab=v2ab=v decides which signs go together. The two square roots are opposites, not four independent sign choices.

Example: for −7+24i-7+24i−7+24i, R=25R=25R=25, so a2=9,b2=16a^2=9,b^2=16a2=9,b2=16. If a>0a>0a>0, then a=3a=3a=3, and 2ab=242ab=242ab=24 gives b=4b=4b=4. The roots are ±(3+4i)\pm(3+4i)±(3+4i).

For a negative real input, the roots are purely imaginary and a=0a=0a=0. For a positive real input, the roots are real. For zero, there is only one distinct root. These cases are why a general shortcut must not blindly divide by aaa.

Square-root warning: for arbitrary complex inputs, principal square roots do not always satisfy uv=uv\sqrt{uv}=\sqrt u\sqrt vuv​=u​v​. For instance, the principal values give −1−1=−1\sqrt{-1}\sqrt{-1}=-1−1​−1​=−1, whereas (−1)(−1)=1\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}=1(−1)(−1)​=1.

Concept C16 — Quadratic roots: conjugates and symmetric expressions

Important for JEE Main. For

ax2+bx+c=0,a≠0,ax^2+bx+c=0,\qquad a\ne0,ax2+bx+c=0,a=0,

with roots α,β\alpha,\betaα,β,

α+β=−ba,αβ=ca.\boxed{\alpha+\beta=-\frac ba,\qquad\alpha\beta=\frac ca}.α+β=−ab​,αβ=ac​​.

These follow by expanding a(x−α)(x−β)a(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)a(x−α)(x−β) and comparing coefficients. They work even when the roots are nonreal.

If the coefficients are real, a nonreal root comes with its conjugate. Conjugating the entire equation proves that if u+ivu+ivu+iv is a root, u−ivu-ivu−iv is also a root. This need not hold for a polynomial with arbitrary complex coefficients.

For a monic quadratic with roots u±ivu\pm ivu±iv,

x2−2ux+(u2+v2)=0.\boxed{x^2-2ux+(u^2+v^2)=0}.x2−2ux+(u2+v2)=0​.

The product is ∣u+iv∣2|u+iv|^2∣u+iv∣2, a positive real number for a nonreal pair.

Recognize a target containing powers of both roots. Set s=α+βs=\alpha+\betas=α+β, p=αβp=\alpha\betap=αβ. Then

α2+β2=s2−2p,α3+β3=s3−3ps,\alpha^2+\beta^2=s^2-2p,\qquad \alpha^3+\beta^3=s^3-3ps,α2+β2=s2−2p,α3+β3=s3−3ps, α4+β4=(s2−2p)2−2p2.\boxed{\alpha^4+\beta^4=(s^2-2p)^2-2p^2}.α4+β4=(s2−2p)2−2p2​.

Why the last subtraction? Squaring α2+β2\alpha^2+\beta^2α2+β2 includes the extra 2α2β2=2p22\alpha^2\beta^2=2p^22α2β2=2p2.

More generally, Un=αn+βnU_n=\alpha^n+\beta^nUn​=αn+βn satisfies

U0=2,U1=s,Un=sUn−1−pUn−2.\boxed{U_0=2,\quad U_1=s,\quad U_n=sU_{n-1}-pU_{n-2}}.U0​=2,U1​=s,Un​=sUn−1​−pUn−2​​.

Each root satisfies t2=st−pt^2=st-pt2=st−p. Multiply by tn−2t^{n-2}tn−2 and add the two equations.

A shorter cycle may exist. For t2−t+1=0t^2-t+1=0t2−t+1=0,

(t+1)(t2−t+1)=t3+1=0.(t+1)(t^2-t+1)=t^3+1=0.(t+1)(t2−t+1)=t3+1=0.

Thus t3=−1t^3=-1t3=−1 and t6=1t^6=1t6=1. Q35 asks for a huge power, so this cycle is shorter than a long recurrence.

Concept C17 — Triangle geometry on the complex plane

Important for JEE Main. Always identify which complex numbers represent vertices and which represent side movements.

For vertices z1,z2,z3z_1,z_2,z_3z1​,z2​,z3​, the side lengths are

∣z2−z1∣,∣z3−z2∣,∣z1−z3∣.|z_2-z_1|,\quad|z_3-z_2|,\quad|z_1-z_3|.∣z2​−z1​∣,∣z3​−z2​∣,∣z1​−z3​∣.

The midpoint of two vertices is (z1+z2)/2(z_1+z_2)/2(z1​+z2​)/2, and the triangle's centroid is

g=z1+z2+z33.\boxed{g=\frac{z_1+z_2+z_3}{3}}.g=3z1​+z2​+z3​​​.

This averages the horizontal and vertical coordinates separately.

An equilateral triangle with side sss has height 3 s/2\sqrt3\,s/23​s/2 and area

A=34s2.\boxed{A=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2}.A=43​​s2​.

Draw the altitude: it halves the base and makes a right triangle. Pythagoras gives the height, then A=12(base)(height)A=\tfrac12(\text{base})(\text{height})A=21​(base)(height).

If two vertices are a,ba,ba,b, the two possible third vertices of an equilateral triangle are

c=a+b2 ± 32i(b−a).\boxed{c=\frac{a+b}{2}\ \pm\ \frac{\sqrt3}{2}i(b-a)}.c=2a+b​ ± 23​​i(b−a)​.

Why? Start at the midpoint, turn the side movement through 90∘90^\circ90∘ using iii, and scale it to the altitude. The two signs put the vertex on opposite sides.

For arbitrary triangles, put u=z2−z1u=z_2-z_1u=z2​−z1​ and v=z3−z1v=z_3-z_1v=z3​−z1​. Then

A=12∣Im⁡(u‾ v)∣.\boxed{A=\frac12|\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,v)|}.A=21​∣Im(uv)∣​.

Indeed, if u=p+iqu=p+iqu=p+iq and v=r+isv=r+isv=r+is, the imaginary part is ps−qrps-qrps−qr, the signed parallelogram area. The absolute value removes orientation; the factor 1/21/21/2 gives triangle area.

For nonzero vvv, u/vu/vu/v real means parallel side movements, so the three points are collinear. If Re⁡(uv‾)=0\operatorname{Re}(u\overline v)=0Re(uv)=0 and both movements are nonzero, they are perpendicular.

For three distinct vertices, the equilateral condition can also be written

z12+z22+z32=z1z2+z2z3+z3z1.z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2=z_1z_2+z_2z_3+z_3z_1.z12​+z22​+z32​=z1​z2​+z2​z3​+z3​z1​.

Use side lengths or the midpoint construction first if this identity is unfamiliar. Distinctness matters: three identical points also satisfy the equation but do not make a triangle.

Concept C18 — Short cycles and weighted sums

Important for JEE Main. Look for what stays unchanged after a fixed number of powers.

If z+1/z=1z+1/z=1z+1/z=1, then z≠0z\ne0z=0 and

z2−z+1=0⟹z3=−1,z6=1.z^2-z+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z^3=-1,\quad z^6=1.z2−z+1=0⟹z3=−1,z6=1.

A large exponent can now be reduced modulo 666. This often avoids finding the two individual values of zzz.

For a reciprocal-power sum, Vn=zn+z−nV_n=z^n+z^{-n}Vn​=zn+z−n,

V0=2,V1=z+z−1,Vn=V1Vn−1−Vn−2.\boxed{V_0=2,\quad V_1=z+z^{-1},\quad V_n=V_1V_{n-1}-V_{n-2}}.V0​=2,V1​=z+z−1,Vn​=V1​Vn−1​−Vn−2​​.

Multiply the two sums to see the neighbouring powers. Use a visible short cycle before computing many recurrence steps.

Weighted geometric sums. A sum such as

S=1+2ω+3ω2+⋯+30ω29S=1+2\omega+3\omega^2+\cdots+30\omega^{29}S=1+2ω+3ω2+⋯+30ω29

has coefficients increasing by one while powers increase by one. Multiplying by ω\omegaω shifts the terms so neighbouring coefficients can subtract:

(1−ω)S=(1+ω+⋯+ω29)−30ω30.(1-\omega)S=(1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^{29})-30\omega^{30}.(1−ω)S=(1+ω+⋯+ω29)−30ω30.

For a nonreal cube root, the bracket is ten complete zero-sum groups, and ω30=1\omega^{30}=1ω30=1. Thus (1−ω)S=−30(1-\omega)S=-30(1−ω)S=−30.

Another useful view is to group three terms at a time. Q34 shows both routes and explains the cancellation explicitly. Do not expand thirty complex terms one by one.

Concept C19 — Two source-question extensions with conventions

Useful supporting connection for Q33. If ∣z∣=1|z|=1∣z∣=1 and z≠1z\ne1z=1, set

w=1+z1−z.w=\frac{1+z}{1-z}.w=1−z1+z​.

Since z‾=1/z\overline z=1/zz=1/z,

w‾=1+1/z1−1/z=z+1z−1=−w.\overline w=\frac{1+1/z}{1-1/z} =\frac{z+1}{z-1}=-w.w=1−1/z1+1/z​=z−1z+1​=−w.

Therefore Re⁡w=0\operatorname{Re}w=0Rew=0. At z=−1z=-1z=−1, w=0w=0w=0. The real-part statement is always true; calling zero “purely imaginary” depends on the convention being used.

Principal complex power in Q33(iv). This is a source-question extension, not a new core formula to memorize without its meaning. For a nonzero complex base, the principal logarithm records its length and chosen principal angle:

Log⁡z=ln⁡∣z∣+iArg⁡z.\operatorname{Log}z=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}z.Logz=ln∣z∣+iArgz.

The principal value of zwz^wzw is defined as ewLog⁡ze^{w\operatorname{Log}z}ewLogz. For iii, length 111 and angle π/2\pi/2π/2 give

Log⁡i=iπ/2,ii=ei(iπ/2)=e−π/2.\operatorname{Log}i=i\pi/2,\qquad \boxed{i^i=e^{i(i\pi/2)}=e^{-\pi/2}}.Logi=iπ/2,ii=ei(iπ/2)=e−π/2​.

This is a positive real number. If all angle branches are considered, the values become e−π/2−2kπe^{-\pi/2-2k\pi}e−π/2−2kπ for integers kkk; they are still real. Keep the chosen convention explicit. Do not extend ordinary real exponent laws blindly to arbitrary complex powers.

Recognize the question model

These are thinking routes, not measured PYQ-frequency ranks.

Visible clue Useful first move Where
Huge integer power Simplify the base; find a short angular cycle. C03, C07–C10
Conjugate in a denominator Multiply by the denominator's conjugate. C04
Only length is asked Take moduli before a full division or expansion. C05
Angle or direction Draw the quadrant; retain principal-angle adjustment. C06–C08
Difference inside modulus Read it as distance between two points. C02, C11
Argument of a quotient Identify both directions; keep the sign choosing the arc. C12
zm=z‾z^m=\overline zzm=z Separate zero, then use lengths and roots of unity. C14
Symmetric root powers Use sum/product or a root cycle before solving roots. C16
Increasing coefficients times powers Shift and subtract, or group a complete cycle. C18

Worked solutions to the 35 PDF questions

Try each question before reading the working. Read the picture and reason for the route, then follow the calculation. The second approaches remain fully included.

Question 1 — Four powers make one complete cycle

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C03

The value of i+i2+i3+⋯+i2023i+i^2+i^3+\cdots+i^{2023}i+i2+i3+⋯+i2023 is

  • (a) −1-1−1
  • (b) 000
  • (c) iii
  • (d) −i-i−i

Notice the repeating group, not the large number 202320232023.

i+i2+i3+i4=i−1−i+1=0.i+i^2+i^3+i^4=i-1-i+1=0.i+i2+i3+i4=i−1−i+1=0.

There are 2020=4(505)2020=4(505)2020=4(505) terms in complete groups. The remaining exponents have remainders 1,2,31,2,31,2,3:

i2021+i2022+i2023=i−1−i=−1.i^{2021}+i^{2022}+i^{2023}=i-1-i=\boxed{-1}.i2021+i2022+i2023=i−1−i=−1​.

Answer: (a). Check: the imaginary terms cancel, leaving a real answer. Do not confuse the sum with just its last term i2023i^{2023}i2023.

Question 2 — Simplify before taking a large power

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C03–C04

The value of (1+i1−i)101\left(\dfrac{1+i}{1-i}\right)^{101}(1−i1+i​)101 is

  • (a) −i-i−i
  • (b) 111
  • (c) −1-1−1
  • (d) iii

Simplify the base first. Expanding a fraction to power 101101101 would hide its simple value. Multiply top and bottom by 1+i1+i1+i, the conjugate of the denominator:

1+i1−i=(1+i)2(1−i)(1+i)=2i2=i.\frac{1+i}{1-i}=\frac{(1+i)^2}{(1-i)(1+i)} =\frac{2i}{2}=i.1−i1+i​=(1−i)(1+i)(1+i)2​=22i​=i.

Now the large power is only a cycle question:

i101=i4(25)+1=i(d).i^{101}=i^{4(25)+1}=\boxed{i}\qquad\text{(d)}.i101=i4(25)+1=i​(d).

Check: the original numerator and denominator have equal lengths, so the quotient must have length 111; the answer does.

Another possible approach — angle difference. Both lengths are 2\sqrt22​. Their directions are π/4\pi/4π/4 and −π/4-\pi/4−π/4, so division gives a unit arrow at π/2\pi/2π/2, namely iii. This is useful when polar form is already clear.

Question 3 — Only the length is asked

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C05

The modulus of 3+4i1−2i\dfrac{3+4i}{1-2i}1−2i3+4i​ is

  • (a) 5\sqrt55​
  • (b) 555\sqrt555​
  • (c) 555
  • (d) 15\dfrac1{\sqrt5}5​1​

What is asked: the length, not the full quotient. A full rationalization works, but it calculates a real part and an imaginary part that we do not need.

∣3+4i1−2i∣=∣3+4i∣∣1−2i∣=9+161+4=5(a).\left|\frac{3+4i}{1-2i}\right| =\frac{|3+4i|}{|1-2i|} =\frac{\sqrt{9+16}}{\sqrt{1+4}} =\boxed{\sqrt5}\qquad\text{(a)}.​1−2i3+4i​​=∣1−2i∣∣3+4i∣​=1+4​9+16​​=5​​(a).

The denominator is nonzero, so the quotient rule is allowed.

Another possible approach — calculate and check.

(3+4i)(1+2i)5=−5+10i5=−1+2i.\frac{(3+4i)(1+2i)}5=\frac{-5+10i}{5}=-1+2i.5(3+4i)(1+2i)​=5−5+10i​=−1+2i.

Its modulus is 1+4=5\sqrt{1+4}=\sqrt51+4​=5​. This verifies the shorter length route.

Question 4 — A tangent does not choose the quadrant

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C06

The principal argument of −3+i-\sqrt3+i−3​+i is

  • (a) π6\dfrac\pi66π​
  • (b) −5π6-\dfrac{5\pi}6−65π​
  • (c) 2π3\dfrac{2\pi}332π​
  • (d) 5π6\dfrac{5\pi}665π​

Place the point before using a tangent. The real part is negative and the imaginary part positive, so the arrow lies in quadrant II.

The small reference angle is

α=tan⁡−113=π6.\alpha=\tan^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt3}=\frac\pi6.α=tan−13​1​=6π​.

Hence

Arg⁡(−3+i)=π−π6=5π6(d).\operatorname{Arg}(-\sqrt3+i)=\pi-\frac\pi6 =\boxed{\frac{5\pi}6}\qquad\text{(d)}.Arg(−3​+i)=π−6π​=65π​​(d).

Check: the angle is between π/2\pi/2π/2 and π\piπ, as quadrant II requires. The value π/6\pi/6π/6 would point into quadrant I. The value −5π/6-5\pi/6−5π/6 would point below the real axis.

Question 5 — A power multiplies the angle

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C07–C09

The value of (1+i3)12(1+i\sqrt3)^{12}(1+i3​)12 is

  • (a) −4096-4096−4096
  • (b) 4096i4096i4096i
  • (c) 409640964096
  • (d) 204820482048

The large power suggests length-and-angle form.

∣1+i3∣=2,1+i3=2cis⁡π3.|1+i\sqrt3|=2,\qquad 1+i\sqrt3=2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3.∣1+i3​∣=2,1+i3​=2cis3π​.

Use de Moivre's formula:

(1+i3)12=212cis⁡(4π)=4096(c).(1+i\sqrt3)^{12} =2^{12}\operatorname{cis}(4\pi) =\boxed{4096}\qquad\text{(c)}.(1+i3​)12=212cis(4π)=4096​(c).

Check: 4π4\pi4π is two full turns, so the output lies on the positive real axis.

Another possible approach — cube once, then use a real power.

(1+i3)2=−2+2i3,(1+i3)3=−8.(1+i\sqrt3)^2=-2+2i\sqrt3,\quad (1+i\sqrt3)^3=-8.(1+i3​)2=−2+2i3​,(1+i3​)3=−8.

Thus the twelfth power is (−8)4=4096(-8)^4=4096(−8)4=4096. This is a short algebraic alternative because the cube becomes real.

Question 6 — Use the cube-root identity before expanding

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C10

If ω\omegaω is a non-real cube root of unity, then (1−ω+ω2)6+(1+ω−ω2)6(1-\omega+\omega^2)^6+(1+\omega-\omega^2)^6(1−ω+ω2)6+(1+ω−ω2)6 equals

  • (a) 646464
  • (b) 128128128
  • (c) 000
  • (d) 256256256

Did you notice the three cube-root terms? Use 1+ω+ω2=01+\omega+\omega^2=01+ω+ω2=0 before taking sixth powers:

1−ω+ω2=(1+ω+ω2)−2ω=−2ω,1-\omega+\omega^2=(1+\omega+\omega^2)-2\omega=-2\omega,1−ω+ω2=(1+ω+ω2)−2ω=−2ω, 1+ω−ω2=(1+ω+ω2)−2ω2=−2ω2.1+\omega-\omega^2=(1+\omega+\omega^2)-2\omega^2=-2\omega^2.1+ω−ω2=(1+ω+ω2)−2ω2=−2ω2.

Therefore

(−2ω)6+(−2ω2)6=64ω6+64ω12=64+64=128(b).(-2\omega)^6+(-2\omega^2)^6 =64\omega^6+64\omega^{12} =64+64=\boxed{128}\qquad\text{(b)}.(−2ω)6+(−2ω2)6=64ω6+64ω12=64+64=128​(b).

Check: ω6=(ω3)2=1\omega^6=(\omega^3)^2=1ω6=(ω3)2=1 and ω12=1\omega^{12}=1ω12=1. A six-power expansion is valid, but it creates terms that the zero-sum identity removes immediately.

Question 7 — Equal distances give a perpendicular bisector

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C02, C11

The locus of the point zzz satisfying ∣z−1∣=∣z+i∣|z-1|=|z+i|∣z−1∣=∣z+i∣ is

  • (a) the line x−y=0x-y=0x−y=0
  • (b) the line x+y=1x+y=1x+y=1
  • (c) the line x+y=0x+y=0x+y=0
  • (d) the circle x2+y2=1x^2+y^2=1x2+y2=1

First translate the distances. The fixed points are A=1=(1,0)A=1=(1,0)A=1=(1,0) and B=−i=(0,−1)B=-i=(0,-1)B=−i=(0,−1), because z+i=z−(−i)z+i=z-(-i)z+i=z−(−i). Points equally far from A,BA,BA,B lie on their perpendicular bisector.

Calculation. Put z=x+iyz=x+iyz=x+iy and square the nonnegative distances:

(x−1)2+y2=x2+(y+1)2.(x-1)^2+y^2=x^2+(y+1)^2.(x−1)2+y2=x2+(y+1)2.

Cancel x2+y2x^2+y^2x2+y2:

−2x+1=2y+1⟹x+y=0(c).-2x+1=2y+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{x+y=0}\qquad\text{(c)}.−2x+1=2y+1⟹x+y=0​(c).

Check: z=0z=0z=0 is distance 111 from both fixed points and lies on the line.

Another possible approach — midpoint and direction. The midpoint is (1/2,−1/2)(1/2,-1/2)(1/2,−1/2). The joining line has slope 111, so its perpendicular bisector has slope −1-1−1. Through the midpoint it is y+1/2=−(x−1/2)y+1/2=-(x-1/2)y+1/2=−(x−1/2), the same answer.

Question 8 — The nearest point of a circle

PDF page 8 | Numerical value | Notes: C05, C11

If ∣z−3−4i∣=2|z-3-4i|=2∣z−3−4i∣=2, then the minimum value of ∣z∣|z|∣z∣ is ____.

Read the circle before calculating.

∣z−(3+4i)∣=2|z-(3+4i)|=2∣z−(3+4i)∣=2

means a boundary circle with centre C(3,4)C(3,4)C(3,4) and radius 222. The centre is OC=5OC=5OC=5 units from the origin.

The nearest point is reached by moving 222 units from CCC towards OOO:

min⁡∣z∣=5−2=3.\boxed{\min|z|=5-2=3}.min∣z∣=5−2=3​.

Check attainment. That point is z=35(3+4i)=95+125iz=\frac35(3+4i)=\frac95+\frac{12}5iz=53​(3+4i)=59​+512​i. It has modulus 333 and centre-distance 222.

Another possible approach — triangle inequality.

5=∣3+4i∣≤∣z∣+∣3+4i−z∣=∣z∣+2,5=|3+4i|\le|z|+|3+4i-z|=|z|+2,5=∣3+4i∣≤∣z∣+∣3+4i−z∣=∣z∣+2,

so ∣z∣≥3|z|\ge3∣z∣≥3. The displayed point makes equality possible. The bound and its equality example together prove the minimum.

Question 9 — Conjugation reflects; a minus sign turns

PDF page 8 | MCQ | Notes: C06–C08

If z1,z2z_1,z_2z1​,z2​ are non-zero complex numbers with ∣z1∣=∣z2∣|z_1|=|z_2|∣z1​∣=∣z2​∣ and arg⁡z1+arg⁡z2=π\arg z_1+\arg z_2=\piargz1​+argz2​=π, then

  • (a) z1=z2‾z_1=\overline{z_2}z1​=z2​​
  • (b) z1=z2z_1=z_2z1​=z2​
  • (c) z1=−z2z_1=-z_2z1​=−z2​
  • (d) z1=−z2‾z_1=-\overline{z_2}z1​=−z2​​

Separate length and direction. Let the common nonzero length be rrr, and choose the stated argument of z1z_1z1​ as θ\thetaθ. Then

z1=rcis⁡θ,z2=rcis⁡(π−θ).z_1=r\operatorname{cis}\theta,\qquad z_2=r\operatorname{cis}(\pi-\theta).z1​=rcisθ,z2​=rcis(π−θ).

Conjugation reverses the second direction:

z2‾=rcis⁡(θ−π)=−rcis⁡θ=−z1.\overline{z_2} =r\operatorname{cis}(\theta-\pi) =-r\operatorname{cis}\theta=-z_1.z2​​=rcis(θ−π)=−rcisθ=−z1​.

Thus z1=−z2‾\boxed{z_1=-\overline{z_2}}z1​=−z2​​​, option (d).

Another useful view — coordinates. The cosine identity cos⁡(π−θ)=−cos⁡θ\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\thetacos(π−θ)=−cosθ and sine identity sin⁡(π−θ)=sin⁡θ\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\thetasin(π−θ)=sinθ give opposite real parts and equal imaginary parts. That is reflection in the vertical axis. Conjugation alone reflects in the horizontal axis.

Question 10 — Check zero before dividing by a modulus

PDF page 9 | MCQ | Notes: C14

The number of complex numbers zzz satisfying z2+∣z∣=0z^2+|z|=0z2+∣z∣=0 is

  • (a) 111
  • (b) 222
  • (c) 444
  • (d) 333

Do not divide by ∣z∣|z|∣z∣ yet: zero may solve the equation. Put r=∣z∣≥0r=|z|\ge0r=∣z∣≥0. The equation is z2=−rz^2=-rz2=−r. Taking moduli,

r2=r⟹r(r−1)=0.r^2=r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r(r-1)=0.r2=r⟹r(r−1)=0.

If r=0r=0r=0, then z=0z=0z=0, which works. If r=1r=1r=1, the original equation becomes z2=−1z^2=-1z2=−1, giving z=i,−iz=i,-iz=i,−i.

There are 3\boxed{3}3​ distinct solutions, option (d).

Check: 02+0=00^2+0=002+0=0 and (±i)2+1=−1+1=0(\pm i)^2+1=-1+1=0(±i)2+1=−1+1=0. A length condition is only a first filter: not every unit-circle point satisfies z2=−1z^2=-1z2=−1.

Question 11 — A conjugate equation becomes roots of unity

PDF page 9 | MCQ | Notes: C10, C14

The number of complex numbers zzz satisfying z2=z‾z^2=\overline zz2=z is

  • (a) 444
  • (b) 222
  • (c) 333
  • (d) 555

Use lengths to reduce the possibilities.

z2=z‾⟹∣z∣2=∣z∣.z^2=\overline z\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |z|^2=|z|.z2=z⟹∣z∣2=∣z∣.

So z=0z=0z=0 is one solution, or ∣z∣=1|z|=1∣z∣=1. In the nonzero unit case, z‾=1/z\overline z=1/zz=1/z, giving

z2=1z⟹z3=1.z^2=\frac1z\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z^3=1.z2=z1​⟹z3=1.

The three cube roots and zero are distinct, so the count is 4\boxed{4}4​, option (a).

Check sufficiency: each cube root has length 111, and z2=1/z=z‾z^2=1/z=\overline zz2=1/z=z. We checked the original condition, not just its modulus.

Another possible approach — real equations. With z=x+iyz=x+iyz=x+iy, compare x2−y2=xx^2-y^2=xx2−y2=x and 2xy=−y2xy=-y2xy=−y. The second gives y(2x+1)=0y(2x+1)=0y(2x+1)=0. If y=0y=0y=0, x=0,1x=0,1x=0,1; otherwise x=−1/2x=-1/2x=−1/2 and y=±3/2y=\pm\sqrt3/2y=±3​/2. Again four points.

Question 12 — Build a square root using two real equations

PDF page 9 | Numerical value | Notes: C15

If −7+24i=±(a+ib)\sqrt{-7+24i}=\pm(a+ib)−7+24i​=±(a+ib) with a>0a>0a>0 and a,ba,ba,b real, then a+b=a+b=a+b= ____.

A complex square root can be built from two real parts. Squaring a+iba+iba+ib gives

a2−b2=−7,2ab=24.a^2-b^2=-7,\qquad 2ab=24.a2−b2=−7,2ab=24.

Also a2+b2=∣−7+24i∣=49+576=25a^2+b^2=|-7+24i|=\sqrt{49+576}=25a2+b2=∣−7+24i∣=49+576​=25.

Add and subtract the two squared-part equations:

2a2=18,2b2=32.2a^2=18,\quad2b^2=32.2a2=18,2b2=32.

Because a>0a>0a>0, a=3a=3a=3. Now 2ab=242ab=242ab=24 gives b=4b=4b=4, so

a+b=7.\boxed{a+b=7}.a+b=7​.

Check by squaring: (3+4i)2=9−16+24i=−7+24i(3+4i)^2=9-16+24i=-7+24i(3+4i)2=9−16+24i=−7+24i. Choosing b=−4b=-4b=−4 would give the wrong sign of the imaginary part; the signs cannot be chosen independently.

Question 13 — Symmetric powers need not require both roots

PDF page 9 | MCQ | Notes: C16

If α,β\alpha,\betaα,β are the roots of x2−2x+5=0x^2-2x+5=0x2−2x+5=0, then α4+β4\alpha^4+\beta^4α4+β4 equals

  • (a) 141414
  • (b) 222
  • (c) −7-7−7
  • (d) −14-14−14

The target uses both roots symmetrically. We can avoid solving for them separately:

α+β=2,αβ=5.\alpha+\beta=2,\qquad\alpha\beta=5.α+β=2,αβ=5.

Notice the square pattern:

α2+β2=(α+β)2−2αβ=4−10=−6.\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta=4-10=-6.α2+β2=(α+β)2−2αβ=4−10=−6.

Square that result and remove its extra product:

p+q=−4+13=9.\boxed{p+q=-4+13=9}.p+q=−4+13=9​.

(z−2−3i)(z−2+3i)=(z−2)2+9=z2−4z+13.(z-2-3i)(z-2+3i)=(z-2)^2+9=z^2-4z+13.(z−2−3i)(z−2+3i)=(z−2)2+9=z2−4z+13.

The sign of ppp is easy to reverse accidentally: the root sum is −p-p−p, not ppp.

Question 31 — A modulus is real, so compare imaginary parts first

PDF page 11 | MCQ | Notes: C04–C05

If zzz satisfies ∣z∣−z=1+2i|z|-z=1+2i∣z∣−z=1+2i, then zzz equals

  • (a) 32+2i\dfrac32+2i23​+2i
  • (b) 32−2i\dfrac32-2i23​−2i
  • (c) −32−2i-\dfrac32-2i−23​−2i
  • (d) 52−2i\dfrac52-2i25​−2i

A modulus has no imaginary part. Put z=x+iyz=x+iyz=x+iy:

x2+y2−x−iy=1+2i.\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-x-iy=1+2i.x2+y2​−x−iy=1+2i.

First compare imaginary parts: −y=2-y=2−y=2, so y=−2y=-2y=−2. Now compare real parts:

x2+4=x+1.\sqrt{x^2+4}=x+1.x2+4​=x+1.

Keep the condition x+1≥0x+1\ge0x+1≥0 before squaring. Then

x2+4=(x+1)2⟹x=32.x^2+4=(x+1)^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\frac32.x2+4=(x+1)2⟹x=23​.

Thus z=32−2i\boxed{z=\frac32-2i}z=23​−2i​, option (b).

Check: ∣z∣=5/2|z|=5/2∣z∣=5/2, so ∣z∣−z=5/2−(3/2−2i)=1+2i|z|-z=5/2-(3/2-2i)=1+2i∣z∣−z=5/2−(3/2−2i)=1+2i.

Another possible approach — use the length as the unknown. Let r=∣z∣r=|z|r=∣z∣. The original equation gives z=(r−1)−2iz=(r-1)-2iz=(r−1)−2i, so r2=(r−1)2+4r^2=(r-1)^2+4r2=(r−1)2+4. This gives r=5/2r=5/2r=5/2 and the same point, with no square-root equation to square.

Question 32 — Products of root sums are exponent bookkeeping

PDF page 11 | Numerical value | Notes: C09–C10

Let z≠1z\ne1z=1 be a 777th root of unity, α=z+z2+z4\alpha=z+z^2+z^4α=z+z2+z4 and β=z3+z5+z6\beta=z^3+z^5+z^6β=z3+z5+z6. The value of αβ\alpha\betaαβ is ____.

The prime 777 and the excluded root 111 give

z7=1,z+z2+⋯+z6=−1.z^7=1,\qquad z+z^2+\cdots+z^6=-1.z7=1,z+z2+⋯+z6=−1.

Expand the product, keeping track only of exponent sums:

αβ=z4+z6+z7+z5+z7+z8+z7+z9+z10.\begin{aligned} \alpha\beta={}&z^4+z^6+z^7 +z^5+z^7+z^8\\ &+z^7+z^9+z^{10}. \end{aligned}αβ=​z4+z6+z7+z5+z7+z8+z7+z9+z10.​

Three terms are z7=1z^7=1z7=1. Reducing the remaining exponents modulo 777 gives each of z,z2,…,z6z,z^2,\ldots,z^6z,z2,…,z6 once:

αβ=3+(z+z2+⋯+z6)=3−1=2.\alpha\beta=3+(z+z^2+\cdots+z^6) =3-1=\boxed{2}.αβ=3+(z+z2+⋯+z6)=3−1=2​.

Check the nature of the answer: β=α‾\beta=\overline\alphaβ=α, since conjugation on the unit circle negates exponents modulo 777. Their product is ∣α∣2|\alpha|^2∣α∣2, so a nonnegative real answer is consistent. A careful nine-cell table is safer than an untracked expansion.

Question 33 — Check a convention and an all-input claim

PDF page 11 | MCQ | Notes: C04, C06, C09, C19

Consider the statements:

(i) If ∣z∣=1|z|=1∣z∣=1 and z≠1z\ne1z=1, then 1+z1−z\dfrac{1+z}{1-z}1−z1+z​ is purely imaginary.

(ii) The product of all nnnth roots of unity is (−1)n−1(-1)^{n-1}(−1)n−1.

(iii) For all non-zero z1,z2z_1,z_2z1​,z2​, Arg⁡(z1z2)=Arg⁡z1+Arg⁡z2\operatorname{Arg}(z_1z_2)=\operatorname{Arg}z_1+\operatorname{Arg}z_2Arg(z1​z2​)=Argz1​+Argz2​ (principal arguments).

(iv) iii^iii is a real number.

The correct statements are

  • (a) (i) and (iii) only
  • (b) (ii), (iii) and (iv) only
  • (c) (i), (ii) and (iv) only
  • (d) (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)

Check every statement and state the conventions.

(i) With w=(1+z)/(1−z)w=(1+z)/(1-z)w=(1+z)/(1−z) and z‾=1/z\overline z=1/zz=1/z,

w‾=1+z‾1−z‾=z+1z−1=−w.\overline w=\frac{1+\overline z}{1-\overline z} =\frac{z+1}{z-1}=-w.w=1−z1+z​=z−1z+1​=−w.

So Re⁡w=0\operatorname{Re}w=0Rew=0. The source counts this as purely imaginary, and intends (i) to be true.

Zero corner case: z=−1z=-1z=−1 is allowed and gives w=0w=0w=0. If “purely imaginary” is defined to require a nonzero imaginary part, (i) needs the additional exclusion z≠−1z\ne-1z=−1. Under that stricter terminology, none of the printed options lists exactly the remaining true statements (ii) and (iv). The unambiguous claim is “has real part zero.”

(ii) The roots of xn−1x^n-1xn−1 have product (−1)n(−1)=(−1)n−1(-1)^n(-1)=(-1)^{n-1}(−1)n(−1)=(−1)n−1. True.

(iii) Try z1=z2=−1z_1=z_2=-1z1​=z2​=−1. Then

Arg⁡(z1z2)=Arg⁡1=0,Arg⁡z1+Arg⁡z2=2π.\operatorname{Arg}(z_1z_2)=\operatorname{Arg}1=0, \qquad\operatorname{Arg}z_1+\operatorname{Arg}z_2=2\pi.Arg(z1​z2​)=Arg1=0,Argz1​+Argz2​=2π.

False as an ordinary equality of principal arguments. They agree only after whole-turn adjustment.

(iv) Using the principal-power definition in C19,

ii=eiLog⁡i=ei(iπ/2)=e−π/2,i^i=e^{i\operatorname{Log}i} =e^{i(i\pi/2)}=e^{-\pi/2},ii=eiLogi=ei(iπ/2)=e−π/2,

which is positive real. True. The other logarithm branches also give real positive values.

Intended answer: (i), (ii), (iv) — option (c)\boxed{\text{(i), (ii), (iv) — option (c)}}(i), (ii), (iv) — option (c)​, with the zero convention above.

Exam habit: an all-input claim can be disproved by one permitted counterexample. A principal-angle identity is a good place to test the negative real axis.

Question 34 — Shift a weighted sum to create cancellation

PDF page 11 | Numerical value | Notes: C10, C18

Let ω\omegaω be a non-real cube root of unity and S=1+2ω+3ω2+⋯+30ω29S=1+2\omega+3\omega^2+\cdots+30\omega^{29}S=1+2ω+3ω2+⋯+30ω29. Then ∣S∣=|S|=∣S∣= ____ (round off to 222 decimal places).

Did you notice the two patterns together? The coefficients go 1,2,3,…1,2,3,\ldots1,2,3,…, while the powers go 1,ω,ω2,…1,\omega,\omega^2,\ldots1,ω,ω2,…. A one-power shift makes neighbouring coefficients subtract.

Write

S=1+2ω+3ω2+⋯+30ω29,ωS=ω+2ω2+⋯+29ω29+30ω30.\begin{aligned} S&=1+2\omega+3\omega^2+\cdots+30\omega^{29},\\ \omega S&=\omega+2\omega^2+\cdots+29\omega^{29}+30\omega^{30}. \end{aligned}SωS​=1+2ω+3ω2+⋯+30ω29,=ω+2ω2+⋯+29ω29+30ω30.​

Subtract term by term:

(1−ω)S=1+ω+⋯+ω29−30ω30.(1-\omega)S =1+\omega+\cdots+\omega^{29}-30\omega^{30}.(1−ω)S=1+ω+⋯+ω29−30ω30.

The first 303030 terms make ten complete zero-sum triples; ω30=1\omega^{30}=1ω30=1. Hence

(1−ω)S=−30,∣S∣=30∣1−ω∣=303=103≈17.32.(1-\omega)S=-30,\qquad |S|=\frac{30}{|1-\omega|} =\frac{30}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3\approx\boxed{17.32}.(1−ω)S=−30,∣S∣=∣1−ω∣30​=3​30​=103​≈17.32​.

Another possible approach — group the triples. For j=0,…,9j=0,\ldots,9j=0,…,9, one block is

(3j+1)+(3j+2)ω+(3j+3)ω2=1+2ω+3ω2=−2−ω.(3j+1)+(3j+2)\omega+(3j+3)\omega^2 =1+2\omega+3\omega^2=-2-\omega.(3j+1)+(3j+2)ω+(3j+3)ω2=1+2ω+3ω2=−2−ω.

So S=−20−10ω=−10(2+ω)S=-20-10\omega=-10(2+\omega)S=−20−10ω=−10(2+ω). Since ∣2+ω∣2=(2+ω)(2+ω2)=3|2+\omega|^2=(2+\omega)(2+\omega^2)=3∣2+ω∣2=(2+ω)(2+ω2)=3, its length is again 10310\sqrt3103​. Triple grouping is especially short here; shift-and-subtract also works for many weighted geometric sums without this three-cycle.

Question 35 — Find the root cycle instead of huge powers

PDF page 11 | MCQ | Notes: C09, C16, C18

If α,β\alpha,\betaα,β are the roots of x2−x+1=0x^2-x+1=0x2−x+1=0, then α2025+β2025\alpha^{2025}+\beta^{2025}α2025+β2025 equals

  • (a) 222
  • (b) −2-2−2
  • (c) 111
  • (d) −1-1−1

A huge exponent does not mean we should find huge powers. Each root t=α,βt=\alpha,\betat=α,β satisfies t2−t+1=0t^2-t+1=0t2−t+1=0. Multiply by t+1t+1t+1:

t3+1=0⟹t3=−1.t^3+1=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^3=-1.t3+1=0⟹t3=−1.

Because 2025=3(675)2025=3(675)2025=3(675) and 675675675 is odd,

α2025=(α3)675=−1,β2025=−1.\alpha^{2025}=(\alpha^3)^{675}=-1,\qquad \beta^{2025}=-1.α2025=(α3)675=−1,β2025=−1.

Thus −2\boxed{-2}−2​, option (b).

Another possible approach — conjugate angles. The roots are cis⁡(±π/3)\operatorname{cis}(\pm\pi/3)cis(±π/3). Their power sum is 2cos⁡(2025π/3)=2cos⁡675π=−22\cos(2025\pi/3)=2\cos675\pi=-22cos(2025π/3)=2cos675π=−2. The polynomial cycle is quicker and does not require solving the roots.
